lesson.title: Zooming In Until the Curve Looks Straight
lesson.summary: Local linearity is the geometric heart of differentiability: near a point where a function is differentiable, the graph becomes visually indistinguishable from its own tangent line the closer you zoom in.
lesson.body:
Differentiability has an algebraic definition, the existence of a finite limit for the difference quotient, but it also has a vivid geometric meaning called local linearity. If f is differentiable at a, then as you zoom in on the graph of f closer and closer around the point (a, f(a)), the curve straightens out and becomes nearly indistinguishable from its tangent line, y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). This is the geometric content of the tangent line concept combined with the definition of a differentiable function: the tangent line is not just a line that happens to touch the curve at one point, it is the straight-line approximation that the curve itself approaches under magnification.

This is also why the non-differentiable points from earlier sections look the way they do under zooming. At a corner, no matter how far you zoom in, the two sides never merge into one line, because they carry two genuinely different finite slopes; the corner just gets bigger under magnification, never straighter. At a cusp, zooming in reveals an ever-sharper point rather than a straight line, since the one-sided slopes are diverging toward opposite infinities. Local linearity is the property those points specifically lack, and it is precisely the property that makes ordinary differentiable points special.

A concrete example makes the zooming idea numerically precise. Let f(x) = sin(x), with a = 0. Then f(0) = 0 and f'(x) = cos(x), so f'(0) = cos(0) = 1. The tangent line at the origin is therefore y = x, an extremely simple line. Now compare sin(x) itself to this line for a value of x close to 0, say x = 0.1. Using the Taylor expansion sin(x) is approximately x minus x cubed over 6 for small x, sin(0.1) is approximately 0.1 minus (0.001)/6, which is 0.1 minus about 0.000167, giving approximately 0.099833. The tangent line predicts exactly 0.1 at that same x-value. The two values, 0.099833 and 0.1, differ by only about 0.000167, a tiny discrepancy considering x itself is 0.1.

Zooming in further sharpens the match dramatically. At x = 0.01, the same expansion gives sin(0.01) approximately equal to 0.01 minus (0.000001)/6, which is 0.01 minus about 0.00000017, a difference from the tangent line's prediction of 0.01 that is now roughly a thousand times smaller than the previous discrepancy, even though x itself only shrank by a factor of ten. This is the signature of local linearity in numbers: the error between the curve and its tangent line shrinks much faster than the distance from a itself, which is exactly what makes the phrase zooming in until it looks straight a mathematically accurate description and not just a visual metaphor.

Local linearity is the conceptual bridge to using tangent lines for approximation, since a line that the curve truly resembles at close range is a line worth using as a stand-in for the curve near that point, a technique made explicit in the next section.
